en: The Sūtra of the Questions of the Youth Sumati, Part One: The Section on Companions, Upper Volume. 1.
The Section on Companions. At that time, the Vajradhara Bodhisattva, the Great Yakṣa General, whose majesty surpasses a thousand suns, with a single-minded focus...
Thus they remained.

Then the Great Compassionate One, the youth Sumāhu, rose from his seat, and having prostrated with devotion at the feet of the Vajradhara Bodhisattva, spoke these words, desiring to inquire about the methods for accomplishing the various vidyās and mantras:

"I have observed those in the world who seek mantras; they restrict their food, maintain their recitations, and practice with single-minded diligence and hardship, yet even through such cultivation, they do not achieve success."
I only pray that the Venerable One will analyze and explain the causes and conditions for non-attainment.

Your venerable majesty is like the brilliant light of the sun; the mantras you expound can shatter all darkness, provide protection, and extinguish all sins. Why is it that when one cultivates the causes, one does not obtain the fruit?
"Even if one practices all the various grades of siddhi—superior, middling, or inferior—as prescribed by the mantras they seek, they will not achieve success.
If one fails to achieve success despite following the Dharma according to the rules, they then abandon the mantra and follow ignorance."
The Buddha taught that through wisdom one attains nirvana, whereas when wisdom is obscured by ignorance, it cannot be cured.
If it is said that a mantra does not achieve accomplishment, it is likewise like wisdom being obscured, for which there is no remedy.
I only pray that the Venerable One, out of great compassion, will expound the mantras to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
If they recite them while also performing the *homa* of protection, why would the Lord of Light not grant them accomplishment?
Is it because the ritual procedures are incomplete, or because one lacks power?
Is it due to the season, or because of transgressions?
Or is it because there has been an addition or omission in the mantras?
"Is it because you lack the requisites for making offerings to the Dharma?
I pray that you will analyze and explain this for the sake of all sentient beings.

When the Vajradhara Bodhisattva, the Great Yakṣa General, had heard these questions from Subāhu, he closed his eyes for a moment in contemplation. He then rotated the exquisite vajra held in his hand, looked upon them with a joyful gaze, and spoke these words:
"How marvelous!
Out of compassion for all classes of sentient beings, you are like the moonlight that shines universally upon the world.
Because this mind of yours is so utterly pure, you have already surpassed all other great bodhisattvas."

A bodhisattva does not seek their own happiness; because they benefit sentient beings, they are able to endure great suffering. Therefore, when a bodhisattva sees the suffering of sentient beings, they themselves suffer; when they see the happiness of sentient beings, they themselves are happy.
I know that your mind is ultimately not for your own sake, but because you wish to benefit sentient beings that you have raised such a question.
Therefore, contemplate with single-minded focus for a moment; I shall now analyze and explain for you the Dharma of the sublime mantra.
"You should listen attentively.
If one is to practice the method of reciting my mantras, it should be performed in this way:
first, arouse profound reverence for all Buddhas; next, generate the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta; and remain far removed from greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and the like."

Furthermore, you should cherish the Triple Gem with great reverence; you must also worship me with sincere and profound respect and honor the Great Vajra Family. You must distance yourselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, harsh words, and double-tongued speech, and you must neither drink alcohol nor eat meat.

If there are sentient beings who practice wrong views, even though they perform wholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind, because of their wrong views, these are transformed into unwholesome ones, resulting in defiled fruits.
For example, when cultivating a field, one must act according to the seasons; yet if the seeds are scorched, they will never sprout.
It is the same with foolishness and false views: even if one performs wholesome deeds, one will ultimately fail to obtain their fruit.

Therefore, one should distance oneself from wrong views and always rely upon right view without wavering; one must constantly practice the ten wholesome dharmas to increase the profound and subtle Dharma.

If there are devas, nāgas, asuras, and other such beings, including those spirits who feed on blood and flesh, who roam the world to harm sentient beings and disturb the minds of those who maintain the recitation, upon seeing one who practices my sublime mantra, they will naturally harbor hearts of terror; for this dharma is utterly incompatible with them.
To prevent those who cause affliction from causing practitioners to regress in their resolve, and to ensure that they do no harm to them, one must enter this Great Samaya Maṇḍala ritual.
Because it is the dwelling place of the great assembly of noble ones and the various devas, it is called the Great Maṇḍala.
Furthermore, one must enter and perform the rites of the Wondrous Maṇḍala, just as one subdues all obstructing spirits, causing them to be tamed.

Therefore, one should enter it diligently and in accordance with the Dharma; likewise, one must enter the great maṇḍala of the most supreme Lord of Light, and one must also enter the great maṇḍalas of the various Lords of Mantras, without interruption.
It is like a vehicle: if it lacks wheels and rims, even if one is a skilled driver, it can never move forward.
It is the same with the precepts that lack superior dharmas; even if one practices them with diligence, they will never increase.
"Furthermore, one who seeks accomplishment must have an excellent companion.

That companion must possess wisdom; they should be pure, upright, and handsome, born into a noble family; they should be courageous according to the Dharma and have subdued their sense faculties; they should speak kindly, delight in renunciation, and be endowed with great compassion; they should be able to endure hunger, thirst, and all manner of suffering; they should not take refuge in other deities nor offer worship to them; they should be intelligent, skillful, and always mindful of kindness and righteousness; and they should maintain deep reverence for the Triple Gem."

One who is thus adorned with such virtuous conduct is extremely difficult to encounter at such a time; therefore, those who possess roots of goodness and virtuous conduct should seek out such a companion.

2. The Second Section on the Classification of Places, Requested by Sumati. "Furthermore, if a practitioner wishes to achieve swift success in reciting mantras, they should dwell in a place where Buddhas have previously resided, or in a place where Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas have dwelt."
In such a dwelling place, the devas, nāgas, and others constantly provide offerings and protection.
Therefore, a practitioner who wishes to purify body and mind and always maintain the observance of precepts should reside in such an excellent location.

If one does not encounter such a land of merit, one should likewise dwell by the side of a great river, or near a small stream, or reside at a marsh; a place where famous flowers flourish and it is far from the clamor of the marketplace, where clear waters flow in abundance and overflow, and which is free from aquatic creatures or venomous insects; or one may dwell in a secluded and tranquil spot among the mountains, where soft grass covers the ground and fruits and flowers abound; or one may stay in the mountain slopes or within rock caves, free from the presence of fierce, terrifying, or venomous beasts.

In such locations as these, one should excavate to a depth of one cubit (*hasta*), thoroughly clearing away all thorns, potsherds, rubble, husks, bones, hair, ashes, charcoal, salt, and the burrows of insects; even if there are deep pits that cannot be completely cleared, they should be abandoned and another site sought.
The place where one has dug should be filled with pure earth, and upon that ground, a ritual chamber (maṇḍala-hall) must be established with extreme firmness.

Because the aforementioned sublime samaya causes the extinction of sins, one should enter it repeatedly; likewise, one should also enter the sublime maṇḍalas of the various messengers (dūtī), as well as the immeasurable lords of vidyās and their consorts.

Having thus universally entered the maṇḍala—the abode of the Lords of Illumination where the masses of merit reside—all the māras, seeing that person from afar, were seized with terror and fled in all directions.

By entering those various maṇḍalas through recitation, this person is protected by the majestic power of the assembly of noble ones. All māras perceive their body as being like vajra and see their dwelling place as a great mass of fire; they all flee in dispersal and are unable to cause harm. Furthermore, the worldly and world-transcending vidyā-lords and mantras will swiftly attain accomplishment.

If one does not enter this great maṇḍala, lacks compassion and the bodhicitta, shows no reverence for the Buddhas, and takes refuge in other external deities, yet still recites and maintains my teachings, they will bring about their own ruin.

If a practitioner of recitation cannot discern how to enter all the maṇḍalas, yet can discern even one samaya therein and possesses deep-seated reverence, they must also enter among the yakṣa classes, as well as the earth-dwelling deities, nāga kings, piśācas, and various malevolent vināyakas and fierce devas; these shall be unable to disturb or harass such a person who upholds the precepts.
For example, although a sprout grows by depending on the earth, it only attains lush growth through diligent irrigation.
It is the same with the sublime Dharma depending upon ethical discipline (*śīla*); by means of this irrigation, the sprouts of virtue are made to grow.
The Dharma of individual liberation taught by the Blessed One consists of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), which one should fully practice.
If one is a layperson, having set aside the monastic robes, all other forms of restraint (*saṃvara*) should likewise be practiced.
Thus, having distanced oneself from defiled phenomena and perfected the roots of goodness, one should expound the gates of the teaching and recite mantras.

If weariness should arise, one should read the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras. Furthermore, for the sake of extinguishing transgressions, one should constantly, in secluded and pure places, construct caityas using either fragrant mud or sand, placing within them the verses on the dharmakāya of dependent origination.

Or, before the relics and sacred images, one should reverently make offerings with flower garlands, incense, unguents, flower lamps, banners, flags, and canopies, as well as through sublime hymns of praise, with a devout mind.
"Constantly performing sacrifices for others—these six dharmas are the fundamental tenets of your tradition.
Furthermore, you should serve the sacrificial fire and serve the king; you must also take a wife, father sons, and perpetuate the lineage."
"You must practice this dharma before you can attain liberation.
How can you recite the mantras of the Śākya teachings?
If the practitioner belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, they will raise this objection:
"You are of the Kṣatriya caste; you ought to perform sacrifices, practice giving, and pursue self-cultivation. These three dharmas are your ancestral tradition."
"Furthermore, you must succeed in subduing enemies; only by practicing this method can you attain liberation.
You should not study such mantras.
If the practitioner is of the Vaiśya caste, they raise this objection:
"You are of the Vaiśya caste, a lowly lineage; you ought to engage in farming, various productions, trade, and similar affairs. It is utterly improper for you to recite mantras."
If the practitioner is of the Śūdra caste, they will raise this objection:
"You are of the lowest caste, the Śūdra; you should constantly offer service to the pure Brahmins. How does such a teaching concern you?"
By means of such various difficulties and afflictions, they disturb the practitioner and cause them to retreat from their faith.
Those non-Buddhists do not merely harm others; they also bring harm upon themselves.

The Dharma of the non-Buddhists involves eating after midday; those who cultivate the Noble Path differ from them in this regard, and for that reason, one should not go to the dwellings of non-Buddhists to beg for alms.

"Regarding the law of cause and effect for good and evil, there is no distinction between the wise and the ignorant, nor between those of the Brahmin caste, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra; this is simply because people in the world engage in false discrimination and conventionally establish the categories of Vaiśya, Brahmin, and Śūdra. If one can cultivate goodness, one shall realize Nirvāṇa."
Even if a Kṣatriya commits a transgression, he cannot escape the evil realms.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, the defiled body of sentient beings cannot attain purity through the purity of food; only by severing evil karma and cultivating various wholesome dharmas can one obtain the purification of both body and mind.

For example, suppose there is a person whose body is afflicted with sores and scabs; he thinks only of being cured and applies medicine to them, ensuring that the pores and orifices do not leak from the "wind of the apertures. His dwelling has doors on the east, west, and north, but none on the south, which should not be left open.
Once the construction is completed, smear the interior of the chamber with cow dung. Then, in accordance with the specific requirements of the ritual, install the sacred image.

As for the representation of the honored one—whether it be painted, carved, or cast—the canvas used for the painting should be made of fine, soft, and closely woven white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) by a skilled artisan; the threads at both ends must be left intact and not cut off.

Since the broad cloth has never been used before, it must first be thoroughly washed and then sprinkled with scented water. The pigments used for painting should not be mixed with glue; they should be placed in a new vessel, and a brush made of cow hair should be used.
The painters should bathe and purify themselves, observing the eight precepts.

They should paint the image according to the Dharma; once the image is completed, one should offer ointments, incense, flower garlands, food and drink, and lamps, and perform extensive offerings including praise and prostrations. Only then will that which is sought be swiftly accomplished.

"Furthermore, if the practitioner is a layperson, they likewise shave their head, leaving only a tuft of hair on the crown; the garments they wear are dyed with red earth, or they may wear white robes, or garments made of grass, or robes made of tree bark or *kṣauma* cloth."

One should also receive and maintain four kinds of alms-bowls—namely those made of wood, iron, or clay—which must be perfectly round and smooth, fine and dense without flaws, and free from cracks or leaks.
One should carry this vessel and wander about for alms.

The place where one dwells should not be far from a village or town, nor too close to a large population; it should be free of non-Buddhist practitioners, abundant in food and drink, and its inhabitants should always delight in giving and have faith in the Triple Gem.

However, there are those who, being covered by the *asmimāna* (conceit of "I") of external paths and relying on their noble lineage, furthermore lack compassion; upon seeing a practitioner reciting the teachings of the Śākya, they become angry in their hearts and disturb them.
If the practitioner is of Brahmin descent, they will raise this objection:
"You are of the pure-practice Brahmin lineage; why do you recite the mantras of the Śākya teachings just as I do?"
"You should study this yourself and teach it to others; you should personally receive offerings and personally perform sacrifices to the celestial deities.

One may also obtain exquisite flowers, such as blue and red lotuses, as well as various other flowers according to one's preference. Recitation is permitted while walking, standing, sitting, or remaining upright, with the sole exception that it is not allowed during sleep.
Having completed the recitation, one should constantly contemplate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and observe their various merits. Chapter Three:

The Section on the Characteristics of Phenomena (*Dharmalakṣaṇa-vibhāga*) in Response to Sumati’s Questions. "Furthermore, all afflictions such as greed that are associated with the mind are called birth and death (*saṃsāra*)."
When afflictions are eliminated, the mind attains purity; the Buddhas declare this state to be liberation.
Just as pure water is inherently free from defilement, yet becomes turbid when dust settles within it, so too is the nature of the mind:
though intrinsically clear and pure, it is rendered turbid by adventitious afflictions that cloud the heart.

"Furthermore, there are many kinds of rosaries to serve as supports: those made of *putrajīva* seeds, lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, *kīśaka*, crystal, bronze, tin, *bodhi* seeds, lapis lazuli, gold, silver, or iron. Taking one such type in a quantity exceeding one hundred, one should hold it with a devout mind and recite according to the Dharma. Holding the beads with either the left or right hand, one should recite with focused intent; using either the right or left hand as appropriate, when the mantra is about to conclude, one should snap the fingers at that moment. One should maintain single-minded concentration in the recitation without error or confusion, fixing the mind upon the Honored One."

Alternatively, one may subdue the sense faculties through mantras and mudrās, sitting upright before the Honored One with an undistracted mind, moving the lips slightly while reciting and maintaining the mantra.

This mind is like the wind, lightning, or a monkey; it is further like the waves of the ocean or a lake—tossing, crooked, independent, and attached to various objects. Therefore, one must collect the mind so that it does not scatter, and recite the mantra.

If weariness, lethargy, or drowsiness arises and causes the mind to become distracted, one should rise to practice walking meditation, or gaze at the four directions, or sprinkle water on oneself to bring about clarity and awakening.
If the practitioner gives rise to a mind of movement or instability, they should immediately apply this remedy:
"This body has no master; driven by karma, it wanders through all realms of existence without any fixed support."

After casting off this body, one receives another form; the karma of evil continues unabated through this process, and one cannot ultimately escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, and despair; the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of encountering the hated, and the suffering of the five aggregates in their fullness—wherever one goes, these are never avoided.
"Stinging insects, gadflies, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst—such sufferings as these exist everywhere.
When the mind desires to turn away from them, one employs these as remedies.
If greed becomes excessive, one should practice the contemplation of white bones.
The practitioner’s eating is also like this: it serves only to eliminate hunger and thirst, not for the sake of enjoyment or gratification.
It is like a person who has entered a deep desert and, driven by hunger and thirst, must eat the flesh of his own child;
the practitioner’s eating is also like this—it serves only to remove the sickness of hunger, and one should not become attached to its flavor.
It is like weighing an object: as the weight shifts, one end of the scale descends; if the object is light, that end immediately rises; if the object is perfectly balanced, the scale remains level.
A practitioner’s eating is just like this: it must not be excessive, nor should it be too meager.
It is like an old house that is on the verge of collapsing; in order to prevent its ruin, one uses pillars to support it.
The practitioner’s eating of food is likewise: it is solely for the sake of sustaining the body, and one must not crave its flavor.
Furthermore, just as one must apply oil to a moving cart, so too, for the sake of increasing wholesome qualities, one must consume food.
For this reason, the World-Honored One taught this Dharma: sentient beings of the desire realm abide in dependence upon nutriment.
The practitioner contemplates the body as being like a plantain tree; he should not crave the flavors of the food and drink he consumes.
Taking whichever one of the four types of bowls is appropriate, he first observes a distance of four cubits before him as he wanders for alms.
The World-Honored One has taught that through wisdom and skillful means one must subdue the six sense faculties and not allow them to become heedless.

Women employ beautiful forms, clever smiles, and coquettish speech; by nature they cherish their dignity, and their gait and gestures are full of seductive allure. This causes the minds of men to become deluded and intoxicated. It is as if there were a mantra spontaneously accomplished by their very nature: it would be better to burn iron pikes with a fierce fire and use them to pierce and beat out both eyes so that nothing may be seen, than to look upon the various beautiful and seductive features of women with a distracted mind.
Go for alms according to circumstances and do not give rise to attachment or dwelling. Subdue the mind through right reflection and enter the homes of others with the conduct of a Muni.

Do not discriminate between high, middle, or low, nor poor or humble families; furthermore, one should not enter places where a woman has recently given birth, places where many people are drinking alcohol, places of dissolute men and women, places where many children are playing, wedding ceremonies, places with vicious dogs, places where crowds gather for discussion, or places where actors perform music. One should not go to any such locations as these.
Having obtained food through alms, he immediately returns to his original place, washes his feet with water, and divides the food into three portions:
one portion to offer to the primary deity, one portion for the unobstructed [spirits], and one portion for himself to eat.

One should eat at the proper times, bathe three times a day, and further offer flowers, incense, and unguents while offering praise; these should not be omitted during the three periods of the day, and the food offered as an oblation must not be defiled.
When reciting mantras, one should sit upon straw mats. If the mind cannot discern the various offerings, one should simply present them while not dwelling with them.
If the practitioner does not contemplate well, they should likewise distance themselves from them immediately; this should be done until not even a single thought remains in the mind.
For example, when a room is already lit, the flame of a lamp becomes even brighter when shielded from the wind;
likewise, when one applies further diligence and vigor in reciting mantras, wholesome dharmas increase in the same way.
"Furthermore, the practitioner should maintain proper deportment."

One must not clap hands, nor engage in music, song, dance, weddings, or gambling, nor go to watch them. Furthermore, one must not slander householders or renunciants, nor harbor pride or arrogance, nor engage in mutual conflict or hostility, nor practice deceit and crookedness. One must avoid sleeping at improper times, engaging in meaningless talk, and studying secular literature or various heterodox teachings. One must distance oneself from anger, resentment, stinginess, greed, vanity, and arrogance, as well as negligence and laziness. One must not drink alcohol or eat meat. Onions, garlic, leeks, chives, sesame seeds, radishes, wild garlic, *buddhina* (translated in Chinese as "donkey-hoof"), and dregs of sesame oil are all forbidden foods. Moreover, one must not consume any leftover food, food offered to spirits and deities, or food intended for ritual offerings.
None of the aforementioned leftover food should be consumed.
Furthermore, the practitioner should diligently spend their days and nights in recitation.
Once the recitation is completed, they should perform the ritual dismissal according to the Dharma.
Spread mats of *kuśa* grass and lie down upon them.

When you wish to sleep, first cultivate the contemplations of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and pay deep reverence with a sincere heart to the Triple Gem and the reliquary stūpas; by means of such practices, you shall extinguish all transgressions.

"Furthermore, the practitioner should consume the 'three white foods,' such as vegetables, roots, fruits, milk, curd, and ghee; or various gruels and porridges made by mixing wheat flour, cakes, oil-cakes, and curd-sauce. If one wishes to achieve the fierce accomplishments (*tīkṣṇa-siddhi*)—such as the rites for *nāgas*, *bhūtas*, *yakṣas*, and the raising of the corpse (*vetāla*), or entry into the palaces of the *asuras*—one should eat sesame-cake mixed with curd-whey."
Chapter Four: The Analysis of the Vajra, Requested by Sumāhu. "I shall now explain the dharma of the *vajra*; those who practice recitation should always uphold it."
Its length should be eight finger-widths, or ten, or twelve, or sixteen; its maximum length is twenty finger-widths.
If one wishes to achieve great nobility and sovereignty, or seeks the siddhi of a Vidyādhara, one should fashion a vajra out of gold.
If the various impure contemplations regarding putrefaction and decay arise,
one should practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion when the fire of hatred is intense,
and the contemplation of dependent origination when ignorance is intense.

Sometimes an enemy turns into a friend, and sometimes a friend turns into an enemy; furthermore, those who have changed from being enemies or friends may again undergo further transformations within their families. Knowing that these friends possess no fixed characteristics, the wise person should not give rise to false attachments.
When the mind desires to go visit friends and relatives during the intermediate period, one must apply this dharma-gate as an antidote.

When wishing to recite [mantras], and after having performed the recitation, one should never engage in conversation with outsiders, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, nor with eunuchs, boys, or girls.
When the religious duties have been completed, if one wishes to speak, one should discuss the wholesome Dharma with one's companions.
Having discarded mucus and spittle, one should then wash and rinse oneself.
Once the robes have been changed, one must bathe thoroughly.

All merits arising from the offering of incense and flowers, the lighting of lamps, the chanting of praises, diligent observance of the precepts, and the recitation of mantras should be dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi.
Just as all streams flow toward the great ocean, and having entered that sea, they become of one taste;
so too it is with the dedication toward Bodhi, for everything gathered together collectively accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood.

It is, for example, like a person who cultivates rice, seeking only the grain and not hoping for the stalks; once the grain has ripened and the harvest has been reaped, the stalks are obtained naturally without being sought.

In this way, a practitioner who wishes to obtain the seeds of merit for the sake of awakening does not seek worldly pleasures; taking unsurpassed bodhi as the fruit, they do not seek out other worldly pleasures—which are like grass stalks—yet obtain them spontaneously.

Furthermore, if there should be someone who, seeking minor benefits, requests [the assistance] of a practitioner, one should not withdraw from one's original vow for their sake, but should answer them with these words:
"Sustained by me, may you obtain a long-lived body and various other requisites; with an insatiable mind, I shall benefit sentient beings and fulfill all their various sought-after wishes."
"Furthermore, one should remain far removed from the eight worldly dharmas, namely:
praise and blame, suffering and pleasure, gain and loss, defamation and fame. These eight worldly dharmas should be avoided, for they give rise to all unwholesome states."

For example, just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, so too, if one performs recitation while ending [the session] with a *kṣaṇa* or a *vajra*, one will ultimately never accomplish any ritual activity.
If one is not capable of discerning this, one should perform the rite accordingly, reciting with single-minded devotion in accordance with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, there are seventeen kinds of articles for the practitioner’s accomplishment, namely:

1. orpiment, 2. ox-gallstone, 3. *añjana*, 4. cinnabar, 5. *tutthaka* incense, 6. realgar, 7. *vajra*, 8. cow’s ghee, 9. *khaṇḍa*, 10. radiant vermilion, 11. chain-mail, 12. armor, 13. fine hempen garments, 14. a single-pronged trident, 15. deerskin, 16. a horizontal sword, 17. a lasso, 18. iron armor, and 19. a three-pronged trident. All such articles of accomplishment as mentioned above are fully endowed with the three kinds of accomplishment."
Even if all the various substances mentioned in other mantra methods do not depart from these three types of accomplishment,
furthermore, there are worldly obstacles and vināyakas who, seeking out faults, pursue the person performing the recitation.
Within this, there are four categories of distinctions.
What are these four?
First, the Destroyer; second, the Jackal’s Fang; third, the Single Fang; and fourth, the Elephant King.
From these four divisions flow forth immeasurable vināyakas.

The leader of the "Destruction" division is named the Great General Aśoka; within his division there are seven asaṃkhyeyas who serve as his retinue. Should there be any who maintain or recite the mantras spoken by the Four World-Protecting Kings, he will create obstacles and difficulties for them.

"In the division known as the Wild (Vanya), there is a leader named Elephant-Head (Gajamukha); within that division, there are eighteen koṭis of followers who create obstacles for those who maintain and recite the mantras taught by Maheśvara."

"The first Lord of the Family is named Ghanṭāpaṭa; his retinue also consists of one hundred and thirty koṭis. Those who maintain and recite the mantras spoken by Mahābrahmā, Kauśika, the Sun and Moon Devas, Nārāyaṇa, Vāyu, and others shall encounter obstacles and difficulties."

"The leader of the host of nāgas is named Śikhaṇḍin; within his host there are ten billion nayutas and one thousand padmas who serve as his retinue. They create obstacles and difficulties for those who maintain and recite the various sublime mantras taught in the teachings of Śākya."
"Furthermore, Hārītī’s son, named Priyaputra, will create obstacles for those who recite the mantras taught by Pañcika.
Moreover, Maṇibhadra’s son, named Pūrṇabhadra, will create obstacles for those who maintain and recite the mantras taught within the Maṇi family."
These various classes of vināyakas each create obstacles within their respective families, preventing practitioners who lack devotion from attaining accomplishment.
When a practitioner achieves success and receives offerings, the Lord of Light (Vidyārāja), having seen this, manifests himself as the lord of the root mantra and returns to his own palace.
"To seek wealth and nobility, fashion it entirely from silver;
for the rite of accomplishing the Dharma of the Sāgara Nāgarāja, fashion it from refined copper;
to enter the palace of the asuras, fashion it from wondrous stone."
If one wishes to accomplish all dharmas, one should fashion [the vajra] by combining gold, copper, and silver;
if one wishes to accomplish the subjugation of yakṣa hosts, it should be made of iron;
and for the sake of obtaining freedom from illness or seeking wealth, one should fashion the vajra from śirīṣa wood or khadira wood.
If one wishes to cure those possessed by all manner of malevolent spirits, one should fashion a *vajra* from *khadira* wood;
if one wishes to accomplish the subjugation of a *yakṣiṇī*, one should fashion a *vajra* from *madhūka* wood;
if one seeks the extinction of transgressions, one should fashion a *vajra* from *aśvattha* wood.
If one wishes to subdue all enemies, one should fashion a *vajra* from wood that harms people;
if one wishes to harm extremely wicked enemies, one should fashion a *vajra* from human bone;
if one wishes to accomplish illusory transformations, one should fashion it from crystal.
If one wishes to cause people to harbor extreme mutual hatred, one should fashion a *vajra* from *kaṭhilla* wood;
for the accomplishment of ghostly beings, or to cause people to wither, emaciate, and engage in strife, one should fashion a *vajra* from *vibhītaka* wood;
and if one desires to accomplish the deities, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras, one should fashion a *vajra* from celestial wood (*devadāru*).
If one wishes to accomplish the rite for gaining the veneration and mindfulness of nāga maidens, one should fashion a vajra from the root of a nāga-tree;
if one wishes to accomplish the rite for transforming one's physical form, one should fashion it from clay;
if one wishes to accomplish the rite for raising the dead, one should fashion it from kātanba wood.
If one wishes to seek wealth, one should fashion [the vajra] from *arka* wood, or *nāga* wood, or *aśoka* wood;
if one wishes to achieve victory over adversaries, one should fashion it from *śirīṣa* wood, or *āmra* wood, or *iṅguda* wood, or willow wood;
if one seeks to accomplish the dharmas of mental aspiration, one should use white sandalwood or red sandalwood to fashion the *vajra*.
Regarding all the various vajra-maces described above, each must be fashioned with five or three prongs; they should be exquisitely refined and solid, ensuring there are no flaws or breakages.
When one wishes to perform recitation, one should make offerings with scented unguents and the like, generate a mind of great compassion, hold a vajra in the hand, and recite the mantra.
When the ritual is completed, one should again make offerings and place [the object] beneath the Venerable One’s feet; it is the same when reciting later.

If one does not hold the sublime *vajra*, there is a *vināyaka* named Black Crow (*Kṛṣṇa*), whose form is exceedingly large. If there is a deficiency in the ritual when offering incense, he emerges from the earth and enters the body, causing various afflictions to arise in the practitioner—namely, stinginess, greed, flattery, crookedness, and anger—and causing him to frequently lose his vital essence, rendering the body impure.

Furthermore, there is a Vināyaka named Dīpaśikhin (Lamp-Crest). If there is a deficiency in the ritual when offering lamps, he immediately enters the body of the practitioner, causing various illnesses to arise, such as heart pain, high fever, and damage to the heart.

Furthermore, there is a Vināyaka named Hasitapuṣpa; if the ritual is deficient at the time of offering flowers, he will find an opportunity to cause various obstacles to arise for the practitioner, such as high fever, nasal congestion, sneezing, tears flowing from the eyes, aching in the limbs and bones, as well as quarrels with companions and their subsequent dispersal.

Furthermore, there is a Vināyaka named Ghaṭakarṇa (Skt. *Ghaṭakarṇa*; Ch. Yánjì). If there is any deficiency in the ritual during the time of recitation, he will seize the opportunity to cause various illnesses to arise in the practitioner, namely high fever, diarrhea, and constipation.

When various vināyakas enter the body, they cause it to blaze intensely and delude the mind, such that one mistakes the west for the east and conceives various distorted thoughts; or one engages in chanting, or desires to wander about without purpose; harboring such heterodox thoughts and being unable to reach a resolution, one then gives rise to false views.

They speak as follows: "There is no such thing as a Great Self-mantra; there are neither heavens nor those who dwell therein; there is neither good nor evil, nor their causes and effects; there is neither bondage nor liberation; thus, for one who recites mantras, their efforts are in vain."

With this wrong view associated with his mind, he spoke these words to deny cause and effect: "When I cut grass with my hand or play with clods of earth, when I grind my teeth while sleeping, or when I give rise to thoughts of desire or the wish to marry, if those whom I love do not love me in return, or if those whom I do not love find pleasure in me, then I shall take pleasure in them."
Feeling neither at ease nor inclined to sleep, he lay down yet could not rest as he desired to engage in unwholesome conduct, remaining awake throughout the night.

Even if he did fall asleep, he dreamed of being pursued by tigers, lions, leopards, wolves, pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, cats, ghosts, jackals, vultures, herons, cranes, and *śṛgāla* (wild dogs). At times he dreamed of people wearing tattered, filthy clothes; at times he dreamed of naked men with shaven heads and blackened bodies; at times he dreamed of naked non-Buddhist ascetics (*tīrthika*); or he saw dried-up ponds and wells, skulls, or heaps of bones.
He formed this thought:
"How is it that the Tathāgata has permitted such a vow—that those who disturb practitioners shall cause their Dharma-attainment to fail?

Regarding such obstacles and hindrances, even if Brahmā, Śakra Kauśika, and the various devas, nāgas, and others were unable to shatter the vow of these Vighnas, there is only the teaching of the Great Illuminating Mantra; by practicing according to the Dharma, one may escape these obstacles."

"Therefore, once the practitioner has completed the prescribed recitations, they should again enter the sublime maṇḍala for the accomplishment of all matters. Having performed this rite, those obstructors and difficulties will immediately retreat and disperse."
"Furthermore, if one performs recitation, offerings, and homa without following the instructions of the Dharma, those [obstructive spirits] will find an opportunity to create hindrances.
Moreover, the practitioner’s mind will constantly waver, giving rise to doubt at every thought: 'Should I recite this vidyā-lord?'"
Or does he recite them?
If one thinks in such a way, that [obstructing spirit] will find an opportunity.

Furthermore, if the practitioner frequently engages in meaningless speech and discusses worldly matters—whether speaking of commerce, agriculture, or fame and profit—such obstructing spirits will naturally find an opening; they will follow at every step, causing the mind to become distracted.

It is like a person walking along the water; their reflection appears within the water, and the form and its shadow follow one another without ever parting. It is likewise with the Vināyakas entering the body of a practitioner—they never depart from it.

Furthermore, there are vināyakas who find an opportunity to enter the body at the time of bathing; some find an opportunity to enter the body when one sleeps with eyes closed; others find an opportunity to enter the body at the time of making offerings.

For example, when sunlight strikes a fire-crystal, fire is produced; likewise, when Vināyakas enter the body of a practitioner at the time of recitation, they cause the mind to become distracted and increase the fires of greed, hatred, and ignorance. Thus it is.

The Vināyakas are called Water-Walkers; if there is a deficiency in the ritual during the time of bathing, they enter the body, causing various ailments to arise in the practitioner, such as hunger and thirst, coughing, indolence, excessive sleep, heaviness of the four limbs, and an increase in anger.

Furthermore, there is a vināyaka named Gandhabhakṣa (Fragrance-Eater). If there is a deficiency in the ritual when offering incense and ointments, he immediately enters the body of the practitioner, causing illness to arise in his abdomen. He causes the practitioner to dwell on thoughts regarding the circumstances of his past lives, or to think of other places; or he causes him to give rise to indolence by thinking of solitude, or to contemplate sensual desires and discriminate among various sensory objects.
Furthermore, four vases should be consecrated in succession; once the ritual procedure is completed, the obstacles to which one is possessed will immediately be liberated.

This maṇḍala is not only able to remove *vināyakas*, but also fulfills the various supreme aspirations of sentient beings—such as those concerning commerce, agriculture, land, men, women, loss, or confusion—and there is nothing among these matters that does not accord with their wishes. Whether it be possession by *piśācas* and *rākṣasas*, suffering from high fever, possession by spirits in children, or being afflicted by spirits that suck vitality, having frequently seen evil dreams, or suffering from all diseases such as epilepsy and the like, once the maṇḍala ritual has been performed and self-consecration has been completed, all such sought-after objectives will be entirely fulfilled. Furthermore, it can eliminate other ailments and disorders, and can also utterly destroy immeasurable karmic obstructions.

5. The Fifth Section: The Analysis of the Signs of Accomplishment, Requested by Soma-hu. "At that time, once the practitioner has attained liberation from all obstacles and difficulties, their body and mind become pure and free from all defilements. They are like the bright moon emerging from the clouds; when the wind blows away the clouds, its radiance shines brilliantly across the heavens."
The same applies to the various merits cultivated by the practitioner: all obstacles and difficulties created by Vināyakas are completely extinguished.

The reason why a mantra might not achieve accomplishment is as follows: it is like a seed that, provided with earth, the proper season, rain and irrigation, and favorable winds, can sprout and eventually reach fruition.
However, if the seed remains within the granary, even a sprout will not emerge, let alone branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit.

Likewise, if one recites mantras without following the ritual rules, fails to make offerings, or lacks purity; or if the syllables of the mantra are added or omitted, or the phonetic characteristics are incorrect, it will similarly fail to accomplish the vast and wondrous siddhis.
For example, when clouds arise and rain falls, the various plants and trees absorb nourishment and flourish, yet the differences in their flowers and fruits—whether large or small—remain unequal;

so too it is with the mantras that are taught: according to the effort exerted by the practitioner who recites them, whether increased or diminished, they obtain a corresponding amount of merit, and the accomplishments attained are likewise of such a nature.

If a practitioner, in a pure location and according to the proper seasons, observes the prescribed rules—even for minor or playful transgressions—such offenses will gradually be extinguished, their mass of merit will become perfected, and they will be able to attain the blessings and accomplishments of the mantra.
If one's transgressions are not extinguished, merit will not arise.

If one does not abide by the Dharma, one will see in dreams destruction, being abandoned by others, or seeing stones being hurled; or one may see terrifying and fearful people holding spears, swords, and various weapons, intending to come and cause harm. One should recognize that such visions seen within a dream are evil omens.
If such signs appear, those Vināyakas will create obstacles and hindrances.

The practitioner should then employ the wrathful lord Mañjuśrī-krodha-vidyārāja to protect the body; by performing the homa as described above, one will be completely liberated from all obstacles and hindrances, which will no longer be able to cause disturbance.
If there are those who recite that mantra, no vināyakas shall ever find an opportunity to cause them harm.

"Furthermore, for one who wishes to remove the obstacles of attachment and attain liberation, they should rely upon this sublime maṇḍala. In a place where cattle graze, or beneath a tree, or at a shrine, or at a crossroads, or in a secluded room, or within a forest, one should construct a maṇḍala using five colors—namely white, yellow, red, blue, and black. It should measure four cubits on each side and be provided with four gates. Within it, one should dig a pit measuring two cubits square; inside the pit, spread *kuśa* grass, and outside the pit, at a distance of two cubits, arrange seats according to their respective positions. Install the Vidyārājas, the Lords of Mantras, and others, and in each of the eight directions, paint the Great Deity of that particular quarter."

Furthermore, take four new vases that are not black, burnt, or raw; fill them completely with scented water, and place within each vase the five precious gems, red lotuses, and branches from various flowering trees. Wrap the necks of the vases with five-colored threads and arrange them in the four directions. Thereafter, one should invite those Lords of Wisdom and others, and worship them with all manner of ritual offerings.
Furthermore, with wine, meat, radishes, and many *pārala* foods, he made offerings to those great deities of the eight directions and to all the *vināyakas*.

Summon that person who is attached to obstacles and cause them to enter the pit, where they shall sit facing east. Then, take the flask that was placed there and, reciting the mantras of the Vidyārāja Cakrīṇḍaka (translated as "Red Form"), the Vidyārāja Kīlikīla, and the Vidyārāja Narabhiṅga, empower the flask by reciting these over more than one hundred times. Sprinkle it upon the crown of their head; thus, they will accordingly enter a dream and see the cause of the obstacle revealed:
either that the syllables of the mantra were added or subtracted, or that the ritual requirements were incomplete.

However, when the various enlightened rulers themselves proclaim this Dharma, those who practice it manifest the breaking of physical marks and signs; yet, like the ocean or a lake, they never fail their appointed time. In truth, these mantras are ultimately neither broken nor severed, nor are they bound together.
For example, suppose there are two close friends, and one of them says to the other friend:
"From this day forward, do not go to such-and-such a house, nor even speak to anyone there."
"Because that person respects such a friend, they do not disobey their instructions, and thus they do not go to them, nor even engage in conversation with them.

The method of true mantras is likewise so; therefore, a practitioner should not destroy the principal deity or the mantra, nor should they sever its bonds, impose prohibitions, or grant or subtract elements from the sublime maṇḍala. One should also not transpose the mantras, nor perform *āveśana* upon them, nor strike or bind them, for the purpose of harming them."

One should not perform homa; nor should one cause damage to limbs or members, nor destroy the host of spirits. Furthermore, one should not cause others to become dull-witted or drowsy; one should not inflict punishment upon dragons, malevolent spirits, and their like; one should not incite mutual hatred in others, nor employ methods of injury, suppression, or binding; one should not treat the afflictions of infants caused by spirits, nor capture or ensnare various classes of sentient beings to cause them harm.
Furthermore, other non-Buddhist schools assert that mantras are accomplished by means of ten factors, namely:

the practitioner, the mantra, the companion, the object to be accomplished, diligent effort, the location, the purified ground, the time, the deity, and the ritual materials; by possessing these ten factors, the mantra is accomplished.
Furthermore, other schools assert that the mantra is accomplished by means of three factors: namely, the mantra itself, the practitioner, and the companion.
Moreover, other schools assert that the mantra is accomplished by means of four factors: namely, the location, diligence, the proper time, and accordance with the ritual rules.

Furthermore, other schools maintain that a mantra is perfected only when five factors are present: namely, the mantra itself, the object to be accomplished, the location, the deity, and the substance.
Thus, these various schools may speak of ten dharmas, or eight, or six, or four, or three, or two; each presents different expositions regarding their fundamental teachings.
However, for this teaching of the Śākyamuni to be perfected, two factors must be present: first, the practitioner, and second, the mantra.

The practitioner must be fully endowed with the precepts, apply correct diligence and vigor, harbor no greed or envy regarding the gains and offerings of others, and remain constantly free from attachment to body, life, or wealth.
The mantra syllables are complete and their phonetic characteristics are distinct; all dharmas that can be accomplished are fully present.
Regarding the abodes of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, where speech is not formed, it should be understood as the reverse of what has been stated above.

"Furthermore, when a practitioner is engaged in recitation, if there is an omission or transgression during the interval, or if there is a break in the practice, or if they abandon the original mantra to be recited and instead hold another principal vidyā, or bestow their own held mantra upon another person—then even if the required number of recitations is completed, it will not be accomplished. One must further perform offerings according to the ritual three times daily, and once the count reaches one hundred thousand recitations, one should immediately perform homa according to the ritual:
using either barley, rice-pollen, or *tila* (sesame) seeds, or white mustard seeds—taking whichever of these is appropriate—and mixing them with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
The number [of oblations] should reach ten thousand, or eighty thousand, or four..."
The three thousand [images] are made of udumbara wood,
or aśvattha wood, or palāśa wood, or nyagrodha wood, or nāga wood, or aśoka wood,
or milrapa wood, or nyagrodha wood, or āmra wood, or khadira wood.
Alternatively, one may take *śamī* wood, *palāśa* wood, *apāmārga* wood, *madhuka* wood, or *jambūka* wood; taking any one of these,
with a thickness like a finger and a length of ten fingers, one should cut both ends of the fuel sticks used for ghee,
honey, curd, and *udumbara* wood, and perform *homa* daily in the prescribed number.
As stated above, once one has restored purity regarding the transgressions previously omitted, one may then seek the *siddhi* of the mantra without any obstacles.

Furthermore, if the practitioner’s own mantra is bound by another reciter of a *vidyā*-lord, or if it is pinned, struck, severed, or broken such that it fails to achieve accomplishment, one must immediately fashion an image of the deity. This should be placed beneath the feet of the respective *kula*-lords of the various families, with their faces turned toward one another. Thereafter, one should recite the great and powerful mantras of the *vidyā*-lords of the various families, such as Kīlikīla, and perform an ablution for the deity with honey and clarified butter (*madhu-sarpiḥ*). After practicing this rite for ten days, that which was bound by others will be liberated.

"Furthermore, if a practitioner performs all the rites prescribed within the mantra without omission yet still does not achieve success, they should fashion an image of that deity using various potent poisons. Then, using the mantras of the Lords of the Families such as Kilikīla and others, they should cut the image into pieces, mix them with white mustard seed oil, and perform *homa* offerings three times daily. In this manner, within seven days, they shall attain *siddhi*."
If they were not established, they would be a pleasure that leads to ruin.

Therefore, all phenomena arise from the mind; they do not manifest spontaneously, nor do they depend on time, nor are they produced by a sovereign deity (Īśvara), nor are they without causes and conditions, nor can phenomena be produced by a self.
It is solely due to ignorance that one wanders through birth and death; the harmonious combination of the four great elements is conventionally designated as "form.
Form is not the self, and the self is not form;
form is not mine, and what is mine is not form. In this way, one should know that the four aggregates are empty.
Form is impermanent, like a mass of foam; feeling is like a bubble; perception is like a mirage; mental formations are like a plantain tree;
and consciousness is like a magical illusion. Such a view is called right view; any view other than this is called wrong view.
"Furthermore, when the number of recitations is complete and *siddhi* is about to be attained, one will see such things in dreams:
either seeing oneself ascending a high tower or palace, or climbing a great tree, or riding a lion, a tiger, or a horse up a massive mountain,
hearing the sound of great thunder in the midst of space, or riding a rhinoceros."
One may obtain a cow, a white elephant, or a bull; or receive wealth, garlands, and clothing;
or obtain wine, meat, and aquatic fruits; or receive red lotuses, scriptures, and honored guests; or obtain a camel together with its calf;
or acquire a fully laden carriage, white thread, a fly-whisk, and a pair of sandals.
Or one may obtain a crosswise-bladed sword, a peacock-feather fan, a golden necklace, precious jewels, or a conch shell;
or one may wound a beautiful woman of refined appearance; or one may see one's own mother; or one may obtain various ornaments for adorning the body, as well as bedding covered with white garments;
or one may see oneself floating across a great ocean, or crossing a river.
Whether at rivers, dragon pools, ponds, or marshes for drinking or bathing; or seeing oneself bathing one's own body with blood;
or seeing [himself] entering a temple, a caitya, or a monastic cell;
or seeing the Tathāgata, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, stainless noble monks, the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, devas, and kings.
Some see great swords, hosts of asuras, or pure brahmins;
some see men and women of noble intent, or wealthy, upright, and virtuous-minded elders;
some see parents and kinsmen gathered together in one place; or some see masters of vidyā-mantras, various sages, and those who skillfully maintain their recitations.
Some see themselves swallowing the sun and moon; some see themselves following after a pit of excrement; some drink human semen and eat human flesh;
some enter a mass of fire; and some see women entering into their own bodies.
Having had such extraordinary dreams as these, one should know that accomplishment will be attained within one month or at least half a month.
This concludes the sixth section on the signs of recitation for the near-attainment of *siddhi*, recorded on the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of Chengli, in the western chamber.
*Sumāhu-jñāna-siddhi*. Recitation Signs, Part Six.
Volume VI, Part 6:
The Section on the Signs of Recitation for Approaching Siddhi "Furthermore, by reciting according to the Dharma, one shall immediately obtain the accomplishment of one's aspirations.

It is like a lion, when pressed by hunger, slaying a great elephant with its immense power; whether it slays a jackal or various small beasts, the power exerted is in no way different from that used to kill the elephant."
The practitioner accomplishes superior, middling, and inferior tasks, and the diligence they exert is likewise of these three grades.

If a practitioner dwells in a place of clamor and bustle, they will be oppressed by various sufferings such as mosquitoes, gadflies, cold, and heat; furthermore, they will hear the sounds of various drums and music, or the singing and dancing of people, or the calls of birds and the sound of flowing rivers, or the tinkling of women’s necklaces. Due to these conditions, the mind becomes distracted; therefore, the practitioner must always remain far removed from such places.

"Furthermore, when the practitioner performs recitation, it should not be too slow nor too fast; the voice should not be too loud, nor should it be too low. One must not interrupt the recitation with conversation, nor allow the mind to wander toward other objects. The phonemes of the mantra should not be distorted or erroneous."

Just as a great river flows day and night, never ceasing for a moment, so too does the merit of the person who recites this, performs offerings, and pays homage and praise to other virtues increase and flow day and night.

When reciting, if the mind wanders toward objects of defilement, succumbs to indolence, or gives rise to thoughts of desire, one should quickly turn the mind back to focus on the syllables of the mantra, or contemplate the deity, or contemplate the mudrā.

For example, when a practitioner of meditation places the mind between the eyebrows and prevents it from becoming distracted, if the mind remains unmoved when objects subsequently arise, that person is said to have achieved success in their practice of meditation.
For one who recites mantras, if the mind remains unmoved at its point of focus, this is called accomplishment.

Therefore, a practitioner who seeks *siddhi* must collect the mind into a single object; when the mind is subdued, joy arises; following that joy, the body becomes pliant (*praśrabdhi*); following bodily pliancy, the body experiences bliss; following bodily bliss, the mind attains concentration (*samādhi*); following mental concentration, there is no doubt in the mind during recitation; following such recitation, transgressions are extinguished; following the extinction of transgressions, the mind becomes pure; and because the mind is pure, accomplishment is attained.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has declared:
"All phenomena have the mind as their root.
Through the purity of the mind, one attains the sublime happiness of humans and devas;
Through the defilement of the mind, one falls into the sufferings of the hells, and even those of animals or poverty;

through the utter purity of the mind, one realizes the state far removed from earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as birth, old age, sickness, and death—a liberation that does not cling to the two extremes and is characterized by quiescence;
and through even a slight degree of mental purity, mantras likewise achieve accomplishment.

One should first receive the offering of impermanence for the Lord of the *iṣṭadevatā* (chosen deity); next, offer to the *vidyārāja* (wisdom-king) of one’s own family; thereafter, offer to one’s own tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Following this, once again arouse the sublime bodhicitta with vast compassion to deliver all sentient beings drowning in birth, old age, sickness, and death. Next, one should sequentially recite either the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, or the *Maṅgalagāthā*, or the *Dharmacakra-sūtra*, or the *Tathāgataguhyaka*, or the *Mahādīpa-sūtra*. Having recited one of these sūtras according to one’s preference, one should then single-mindedly perform the binding of the eight directions—binding the boundary of the eight directions, as well as the boundaries of space and earth—and furthermore, armor oneself with mantras.

Regarding the various maṇḍalas described above, one may create any one of them using pure pigments as desired; however, it is essential to install the deities who protect the eight directions, for they are capable of subduing all obstacles from every quarter.
Next, one should further use the Lion-Throne Vidyārāja to recite over its throne and install it within the maṇḍala.

Regarding the method for protecting the body: take the object that has been prepared and place it upon that ground; while holding and reciting over that object, after a short while, sprinkle it with scented water and perform one thousand homa offerings according to the appropriate rite.

First, take three *aśvattha* leaves and place the object to be accomplished upon them; then, take four more leaves and cover the object with them. Thereupon, recite the mantra with focused mindfulness according to the ritual rules until three signs appear:
increase, vapor, and light. In this sequence, one will accomplish the three types of *siddhi*.
If the breath emerges, that is *siddhi*, and all people will revere and remember you.
If the flame emerges, it is the *siddhi* of transforming one's form.
If the light emerges, one becomes an accomplished *vidyādhara* sage, attaining a pure and subtle body.
It is like the arrival of death, when the sensation of cold pervades the entire body; it is also like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) entering the womb.
Just as sunlight striking a fire-gem causes fire to emerge, so too does the *siddhi* enter the body; this is called the method of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

If one accomplishes the rite through internal means, its signs will appear and *siddhi* will be attained immediately; that is, one sees the flower garland on the image move, or the eyebrows move, or the various necklaces adorning the body move, or sees various celestial flowers in the air moving in a gentle breeze, or a fine rain falls, or feels the earth tremble, or hears a voice from the sky saying:
"Now speak the wish you seek."

Or one may see the flame of the lamp increase, its color glossy and radiant like golden light; or again, when the oil is exhausted, the lamp’s light increases even further. Upon seeing such signs as these, one attains *siddhi*.

Some may perceive the hairs of their white brows standing on end; some may hear the sound of celestial music in the air, or the sound of the necklaces of the devas; or they may behold the Honored One in the sky.
"Furthermore, I shall now explain the accomplishment of the near-siddhi.

Regarding the practice of recitation, one should do so with a heart of extreme devotion, without being distracted by objects of defilement, and free from the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, or heat. One's mind shall not waver before external signs of adverse conditions; even gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, and other venomous insects will not dare to harm them, nor will piśāca ghosts, pūtana demons, and other such classes of spirits dare to approach or pass by."

The verbal instructions that emerged from within the practitioner’s shadow were all faithfully accepted; his intelligence grew ever more acute, he became skilled at composing literary works, and he became increasingly adept in various scripts and calculations. His mind delighted in wholesome dharmas, and he applied himself with diligence and vigor to tranquil conduct.
Furthermore, he saw Kṣitigarbha, who likewise had no bodily illness or impurities, and whose body was fragrant.

If anyone sees him or hears his name and gives rise to a mind of reverence, even if alluring women come of their own accord to call out his name, because his mind is pure, he has no thoughts of desire or defilement.
In the midst of space, one hears the speech of the devas and beholds their forms, as well as those of the gandharvas and yakṣas.

When the reciter perceives such superior and auspicious signs, he should immediately know for himself: "I am now close to the siddhi of the mantra. He must then proceed to perform the rites for accomplishment.

"Furthermore, when a practitioner begins the commencement of *siddhi*, they should observe the eight precepts for two or three days, and must also abstain from food; only then may they initiate its accomplishment."
At that time, the youth Subāhu addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Venerable One, you previously stated that purity is attained not by means of food; why then do you now say that one must abstain from food?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Eating is like oiling a cart.
I do not yet understand what is meant by "fasting"; how is that matter to be understood?
The Bodhisattva Vajradhara addressed Miao-zhen with a voice like the sound of thunder, speaking thus:

"It is not for the sake of purifying the mind that one is instructed to abstain from food; rather, it is because all sentient beings are bound by skin to their blood, flesh, brain, liver, intestines, kidneys, lungs, fat, phlegm, membranes, excrement, and urine—constantly discharging various impure and foul substances—and because such a body is established through the provisional combination of earth, water, fire, and wind."

It is as if four venomous snakes were placed in a single basket; one might fasten them so that their excrement, urine, mucus, saliva, blood, and brain matter—being foul and putrid—do not leak out, but it is not for the sake of obstructing the path that they are made to fast.

If a practitioner gives rise to thoughts of lust, they should observe with wisdom this impure body as described above; thus, the desire that arises will immediately be extinguished, and one will have no attachment to body, life, or wealth.

Once the practitioner has completed the new mantra ritual and realizes that his own accomplishment is not far off, he should, on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the waxing moon, purify the ground by smearing it with cow dung (gomaya). Next, he should offer incense and other perfumes along with hymns of praise, first making offerings to the Buddha;
thereafter, he should further offer flowers, and likewise lamps.
If you wish to know how to act in accordance with the Dharma, even to the point of explaining various matters within dreams as previously described, you should fully practice the *adhaḥsīna* rite.

If [the deity] still does not descend, you should fast for one day, observe the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), and generate great compassion. Then, either before a *caitya* or before a majestic and dignified image, take the mantra of the *kula-mātṛ* or the mantra of the *kula-nāyaka*, and perform this ritual of subduing through recitation. You must be extremely focused; you must not move your body, nor your eyes or eyebrows. Sitting upon *kuśa* grass, you should complete ten lakṣas or twenty lakṣas of recitations, or until you feel it is sufficient in your mind.
If one performs this rite and invokes me with the syllable Oṃ, even a withered tree would enter [the mandala], let alone a human being.

If one wishes to cause [the deity] to descend into a youth, one should select ten, or eight, or seven, five, four, three, or two individuals who are twelve or ten years of age; whose veins, blood, and all joints are not visible; who are perfectly formed and complete; whose eyes are upright and the whites and irises are clearly distinct, like teeth that are white, even, and closely set; whose fingers are slender and long without gaps; whose shins, upper arms, wrists, and calves are rounded; whose breasts are high and prominent; whose thighs and limbs are well-proportioned; whose body hairs grow one by one; whose hair is black and dense; whose navel is deep and waist is slender; whose hearts possess the three internal substances; whose physical marks are fully endowed; and whom anyone who sees them feels love and joy in their heart.

If one obtains such a boy or girl, on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed for purification, wearing new white garments, and having been granted the eight precepts, one should have them fast that day and sit before the explained maṇḍala. Then, one should immediately make offerings to the primary deity, the great deities of the eight directions, and the various classes of asuras and other spirits, using flowers, burning lamps, unguents, incense, and various kinds of food and drink.

Furthermore, having repeatedly scattered exquisite flowers over that youth and anointed his body and so forth, he then held a censer in his hand and, with it upon his head, performed the recitation. First, the syllable *hūṃ* was placed at the beginning of the mantra; in the middle, one should utter the phrase *kṛṣṇahana*, which means "to seize"; then one utters *abhiśa*, meaning "pervasive entry"; and finally one utters *kṣipra*, meaning "swift."
Once the *sīna* has descended, these signs immediately appear: the eyes become joyful, one gazes at objects without blinking, and there is no inhalation or exhalation.
One should then know that the *sīna* has descended. Immediately, one should offer *argha* water and incense, mentally recite the supreme vidyā-mantra, and respectfully inquire:
"O Venerable One, what kind of being are you?"
Any doubts one may have regarding oneself or others should be promptly asked.
That Honored One is surrounded by his retinue; one should then take flowers and fill a clean vessel with scented water, further placing five jewels within it—this constitutes the *argha* offering.

One should then perform offerings associated with praise, with profound reverence, kneeling and prostrating oneself; according to the measure of one's original merit, one should then make petitions for vows.
Once the vows have been granted, one should worship with joy.

Furthermore, having made offerings and offered praises with *argha*, one should recite the held mantra in their presence; thereafter, one should perform the ritual dismissal according to the dharma. Such is the procedure for all mantra rites.

8. The Eighth Section on the Inquiry of Adhobhāṣiṇa Sūmahu. “If one wishes to inquire about matters concerning Adhobhāṣiṇa, one should invoke [the deities] in such places as follows: namely, a finger, a copper mirror, clear water, a horizontal sword, the flame of a lamp, a jeweled ground, the open sky, a sacred image, a youth, a pearl, a mass of fire, a stone, and so forth.”

Having invited [the deity] from beneath the Paṭṣina tree at such a place, one should cause him to speak for oneself concerning matters of heaven and humanity, as well as the past, future, and present—transcending the three periods of time—including all matters of good and evil, each explained in full detail.

If one hears the Dharma but does not rely upon it; if there is an increase or decrease in the number of syllables of the mantra; if one has not completed the recitation; if one lacks right faith; if one does not make offerings; if it is performed on an impure site; if the weather is not clear; or if the physical condition of the youth (kumāra) is either superior or inferior—due to such faults as these, the *siddhi* will not descend.

If one wishes to summon [the deity] down, one should first recite the *sīna* mantra. Upon completing the recitation, on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should fast for that day. Having smeared the ground with *gomaya* (cow dung) so that it resembles the shape of a cowhide, one should then have a youth bathe until pure, clothe him in new white garments, and seat him upon it, making offerings of flowers, incense, and other such items.
One should likewise sit upon a mat of *kuśa* grass within, facing east.

If one wishes to have those matters viewed from below the surface of the mirror, one should first take that mirror and wipe it clean with the ashes of the *homa* performed by a *brahmacārin* Brahmin, perhaps seven or eight times up to ten times. Immediately placing it within the maṇḍala and looking upward from its center, the mundane and supramundane affairs will appear within the mirror.
If one further wishes to apply a horizontal blade, the method is likewise as with the mirror.
If one wishes to examine what has been applied to the fingers, first wash one's own fingertips with purple-rough rice water, and afterwards smear them with fragrant oil.
If one wishes to have them look down into water, pour purified filtered water into a flask; thereafter, the youth shall see the matter therein.
If one wishes to have them look down at an open space or at pearls, sprinkle it with pure water.

If one wishes to cause [harm] at the site of a sacred image by personally killing a precept-observing, pure bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, or by burning a monastery, even if such a person exerts themselves with diligent effort, they will not achieve success because of having committed this transgression.
Regarding those who harbor harmful intentions toward the Triple Gem and cause even slight injury to them, I shall now briefly describe the retribution they receive.
Such persons fall into the Avīci Hell; once they emerge from there, due to their unwholesome karma, they are born into poor and lowly families.

Although one may initially resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, if they later return to prostrating to the gods of non-Buddhist paths, those deities will instead give rise to anger and malice toward that person; consequently, their recitation of mantras will never achieve accomplishment.

From the moment they have resolved upon bodhicitta, they should be venerated by devas and humans; they likewise shoulder the burden of all sentient beings, bestow fearlessness upon them, and ensure the succession of the Three Jewels.
Therefore, one should not prostrate to the various devas, nor perform acts of violent harm, nor kill sages, nor destroy the mantras of the True Lords.
Out of a mind of anger, one should no longer make offerings to the assembly.
One should not, without cause, cut or damage grasses and trees with the hands, nor tread upon lotuses or various mudrās with the feet, nor even prostrate to them.
Yakṣas and other such beings consume offerings and the food used for sacrifices to spirits and deities, or they eat food discarded upon the ground;
or they engage in unrighteous acts toward animals, or commit unrighteous deeds with women in secluded places;
or, out of ignorance, they capture various snakes using nets, or ride them.
When one strikes elephants, horses, dogs, oxen, or donkeys with a staff in order to make them go away,
yet fails to arouse compassion toward those who are ill or beset by suffering, [one commits an offense].
For such people as these, mantras will not be accomplished.

Just as space can never be measured, so too it is with those who, regarding the Triple Gem, act with the intent to benefit but instead cause harm; their acquisition of good or evil retribution is likewise thus.

Furthermore, those who injure sentient beings through nets, snares, and various other means; or who keep puppies, rams, and the like; or who confine parrots and various other birds in cages—such persons shall achieve no success in either this life or future lives.

Therefore, one should not enjoy offerings made to the World-Honored One; nor should one tread upon the food offered to him, nor eat food that has fallen to the ground after being stepped on. One should not carry offerings upon one's head. One should not prostrate before Maheśvara, the sun and moon deities, Agni, or Nārāyaṇa; even if one encounters suffering, one should still not prostrate to them. One should not study or recite the teachings they proclaim, nor should one make offerings to those who practice their dharma.
He shall himself explain therein the matters of the three periods of time, such as gain and loss, as well as suffering and pleasure;
you should accept and uphold the teachings you hear with joy, and harbor no doubts.
When the matters you have asked have been concluded, dispatch [the messenger] immediately.
If this rite is performed correctly, Piṇāka will descend swiftly.
If it is not performed according to the Dharma, success will not be attained, and one will be ridiculed by others.

"Furthermore, as Śīna descended, those youths had cheerful countenances and lustrous complexions; their eyes were wide and long, with a slight reddish hue surrounding the black pupils. They possessed the physical marks of greatness in their spirit and demeanor, and their inhalation and exhalation ceased while their eyes did not blink."
One should know that this is truly a *piśāca*.

If it is a *māra* or one of the lower classes, there is a distinct characteristic: its eyes are red and round, like those of a person looking with anger; the eyeballs do not roll, the mouth is agape in terror, there is no inhalation or exhalation, and the eyes do not blink.
One should immediately understand that yakṣas and other such beings must be swiftly expelled.

If they refuse to depart, one should then recite the verses of Mañjuśrī, or the mantra of the Impure Wrathful Vajra, or the mantra of the messenger Haṃsinī, or the Vajra mantra, or read the Mahāsannipāta Dhāraṇī Sūtra.

If, after reciting as described above, [the obstacle] does not depart, one should immediately perform a hundred homas with *arka* wood or *palāśa* wood, using the Mantra of the Lion Throne (*siṃhāsana*) together with the appropriate offerings.
Alternatively, one may use sesame seeds, or rice-ear blossoms mixed with ghee and honey, performing a homa of one hundred repetitions.
At the conclusion, perform the homa seven times—or at least three times—with the mantra of Kuṇḍalī, and then depart.
The wise who well understand such sublime Dharma and are further able to practice it accordingly, one by one, will achieve accomplishment before long, without excessive toil.

Chapter Nine: The Section on Distinguishing Obstacles and Prohibitions From the *Sūmuhukumāraparipṛcchāsūtra* Furthermore, those who seek siddhi by killing an Arhat, killing their father or mother, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, or shedding the blood of a Buddha out of a mind of malice, shall never achieve accomplishment.

Furthermore, destroying a stūpa, killing a bodhisattva, defiling one’s mother or an arhat, inciting others to kill, and stealing the property of the Saṃgha—whether it be small or great—the World-Honored One has declared these five types to be ānantarya (immediate) offenses.
If one commits this offense, one shall suffer in the Avīci Hell for one kalpa.
Even if one were to diligently recite mantras with great hardship, one will ultimately never attain accomplishment.

Furthermore, to damage the subtle and wondrous sutras spoken by the Buddhas through a mind of anger—whether by setting them on fire, casting them into water, or slandering the Dharma—is what is meant by "improper discernment. One should not engage in fighting with elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, or similar creatures, nor should one cause men and women to wrestle or box, nor go to watch such performances as these; this is called "right mindfulness."

He does not engage in talk concerning kingdoms or territories, nor talk of battles, wrestling, or courtesans; nor does he speak of riddles, nor of past events, nor of defiled matters regarding household affairs.
