When a practitioner recites mantras according to the ritual methods, from the time they begin until the attainment of accomplishment, they must not enter cities, villages, birthplaces, monasteries, stūpas, or the shrines of non-Buddhist heretics, nor should they go to their dwellings, gardens, groves, ponds, or rivers; to such places as these, one should never go.

Furthermore, if one does not obtain the aforementioned sublime and superior abodes, one should dwell in a deserted shrine, or beneath a tree, or by a riverbank, or on a mountainside, or at a spring, pond, or grove, or in a solitary place, or in an empty room, reciting with single-minded devotion.

Alternatively, throughout the year—excluding the period of the *varṣā* retreat—one may travel at will during the two seasons of spring and autumn, reciting with single-minded devotion in mountain forests, by riversides, at springs and ponds, or in empty dwellings.
For example, just as a bhikṣu observes the summer retreat (varṣā), so it is for one who recites mantras.
Even if the practitioner has completed the full number of recitations, they must not perform rites of accomplishment once the summer retreat has arrived.
Continue the recitation as before without interruption; after the summer retreat (*varṣā*) has concluded, one may achieve success only after protecting oneself according to the Dharma. 10.

The Section on the Classification of Homa (Sūmahu-vibhāga-homa-bhāga), the Tenth. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the different methods for establishing the hearth (*kuṇḍa*) for the various types of *homa*."
It may be made circular, triangular, square, or in the shape of a lotus; all must have a foundation.
The mouth of the furnace should be provided with a rim, smoothed and polished with clay until fine and slippery, and the outer foundation and steps must all be firmly constructed.
For performing virtuous deeds, seeking wealth, causing others to hold one in respect and mindfulness, or practicing rites for pacification (śāntika), the hearth must be circular.
If one seeks the accomplishment of all matters, or seeks women, youths, and the like, the hearth must be fashioned in the shape of a lotus.
If one performs rites of malevolent action, such as causing someone to flee or the like, the hearth must be triangular.

If one wishes to subjugate nāgas and other classes of spirits, or to cause them to be burned by fire or to suffer pain, the hearth must be square; its base, rim, and interior should be smeared with *gomaya* (cow dung).
Furthermore, spread *kuśa* grass over the base; likewise, smear *gomaya* (cow dung) four times around the perimeter below the steps, covering it entirely with *kuśa* grass.
Place the materials for the *homa* offering upon the base, and place flowers at the locations where the *gomaya* has been smeared, both above and below the base.
One should not give rise to anger toward those dharmas, nor should one rejoice in the practice of them, nor should one recite their mantras or offer praise.

Even if one possesses wealth, one should bestow it with compassion; first, one should prostrate to all the Buddhas and their abodes, then pay homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and finally pay homage to the assemblies of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
For example, although the new moon is not yet full, all people nevertheless pay it respect and prostrate before it.
So too is the Bodhisattva: although they have not yet awakened to fullness, they will gradually become the full moon of Bodhi.
Therefore, one should pay homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas; they bear the burden of all sentient beings and give rise to great compassion for the sake of their deliverance.
How could any foolish or inferior sentient being be unwilling to pay such homage?
Those bodhisattvas possess inconceivable supernormal powers and are endowed with great diligence.
If one does not pay them homage, not only will the mantras fail to be accomplished, but it will also constitute an act of slandering the Buddhas.
For example, just as fruit is produced from flowers, the flower is like the bodhisattva and the fruit is a metaphor for bodhi.

Although a bodhisattva may manifest sensual desire to those who indulge in desire, manifest harshness to those who are stubborn, and manifest compassion to those who are gentle, that bodhisattva is in reality free from both hatred and love. How, then, could one not pay homage to such bodhisattvas?

Furthermore, by means of various forms of mantra-lords, they are able to fulfill the hearts of all sentient beings according to their respective types; moreover, they are able to fully comprehend all karmic fruits. For these reasons, one should pay homage to the Venerable Master of Mantras.

11. The Eleventh Chapter: The Analysis of the Factors of the Noble Path, Requested by the Youth Sumaṅgala Furthermore, the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path shall now be explained: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This is the path traversed by all Buddhas; those who practice this path shall achieve success in their mantras and further be reborn in the most excellent and sublime realms among humans and devas.
Because the Buddhas of the past traversed this path, they attained equal and perfect enlightenment; it is likewise for those of the present and the future.

The merit cultivated through the actions of body, speech, and mind always relies upon the authentic teachings and never gives rise to negligence or weariness; practicing in this manner is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
To always maintain contentment regarding food, clothing, bedding, and medicine, and not to give rise to attachment toward them, is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).

Not praising oneself, not disparaging others, and remaining far removed from all faults—avoiding them as one would a blazing fire or a ferocious beast—and always delighting in tranquility: this is called right speech.

Not studying divination for good or bad fortune, matters concerning men and women, astronomy and geography, methods for training elephants and horses, the arts of archery, calligraphy, and arithmetic, or worldly discourse and useless scriptures—staying far removed from such faults is called right view.
It is said that one who does not follow the ritual rules not only fails to achieve success, but will also bring harm upon themselves.

However, even if the practitioner reciting the mantra does not follow the rules, the Lords of the Mantras will ultimately never inflict harm; it is their attendants who, seeing such transgressions, will instead inflict harm.

"Furthermore, if one wishes to perform recitations and attain accomplishment, and to carry out various rites without obstacles so as to swiftly achieve *siddhi*, one should offer various foods and drinks as sacrifices to the devas, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, garuḍas, jīvañjīvakas, kaṭapūtanas, gandharvas, bhūtas, and all manner of malevolent spirits—whether they dwell upon the earth or in the void. The practitioner, with the right knee touching the ground, should address them, saying:
'O hosts of devas and bhūtas who dwell on Mount Sumeru; those who reside in the Nandana Grove and other celestial palaces;
those who dwell in the palaces of the sun and moon, the seven golden mountains, or by the rivers and on the seashores;'"
In marshes, or in springs and wells; or in villages and various shrines;
or in empty rooms, or in celestial chambers; or in monasteries, or on stūpas;
or in the grass huts of non-Buddhists, or in elephant stables; or in storehouses, or in streets and alleys; or in...
Whether at crossroads, or dwelling beneath solitary trees, or on great highways,
or among burial mounds, or in vast forests, or in places frequented by lions and tigers, or on great deserts,
or in sublime locations upon various islands— they all give rise to joy and descend together with their retinues.

As I approach this place, I have prepared flower garlands, unguents, incense, food and drink, as well as exquisite lamps; may you deign to partake of them, and may the fruits of my aspirations be fulfilled.

Having thus made offerings to the various spirits and ghosts, one should on a subsequent day separately make offerings to the deities who protect the directions. Preparing the offerings as previously distinguished, one should kneel with palms joined and address them with this invitation:
"I respectfully invite the Deva Kauśika of the eastern direction, together with your retinue, to descend here; may you graciously accept these offerings which I present."

Next, in the southeast, invite the Celestial Deity of Fire; next, in the south, invite Yama; next, in the southwest, invite the Great King Nirṛti-piṅgala; next, in the west, invite the Nāga King Varuṇa; next, in the northwest, invite the Wind Deity King; next, in the north, invite the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; next, in the northeast, invite Īśāna; and next, in the zenith, invite the Brahmā Deity King and others. With whatever substances of fragrant ointment and so forth have been prepared, make offerings to the Three Jewels, the presiding deity of the respective family, as well as the Lords of Vidyās and the Lords of Mantras.

Once the fire has been fanned into life, one should not blow upon it with the mouth; rather, using rice, ghee, or sesame mixed with ghee, one should perform *homa* seven, eight, ten, or even twenty times with the principal mantra of the deity, thereby making offerings to the Lord of the Mantra.

Spread mats of *kuśa* grass and sit facing east; place *sūmi* and curd together in a single vessel, and cap the top of the *homa* wood with it. Then, for the sake of accomplishing the root mantra, perform the *homa* according to the ritual rules.
Within that fire, one should observe the signs of accomplishment or non-accomplishment by means of the sound of the crackling flames.

If the fire is smokeless and its flames are golden in color; if the rising flames swirl and turn to the right and their crests are numerous; if their color is white, or like red, or turns a deep crimson like coral; if the appearance of the color is glossy and moist; and if after the flames rise upward, they flow back down and broaden, or like the moonlight of a white moon; [then these are signs of accomplishment].

The shapes of its flames are like those of vases, banners, parasols, and auspicious *śrīvatsa* symbols; they take the form of the *svastika*, or like conch shells and lotuses; or they resemble *homa* ladles, *triśūlas*, and *vajras*; or like horizontal swords, bundles of grass, or the shape of a chariot; or like a fly-whisk.
Their sounds are like those of flutes, *pi-pa*, and *li-er* pipes—various musical tones—or like the sound of a conch shell.
Its fragrance is like the scent of burning *ghee*, yet it is not acrid or pungent. This fire ignites spontaneously without being fanned.
When such signs appear, one will certainly attain vast accomplishment.
Alternatively, many flames may arise, yet they are fierce and violent; these flames are difficult to ignite, and even if ignited, they do not increase, but rather suddenly extinguish themselves.
It is as if there were no fire at all; the color of the flames is withered and parched, black like dark clouds, resembling *pārśa* wood.
Its form is like that of a *yakṣa*, a winnowing basket, a male organ, or the horn of a bull;
its sound is like the braying of a donkey; its fire erupts and burns the person performing the recitation; and its odor is like the smell of a cremated corpse.
When such signs appear, success will not be achieved.

Upon seeing these inauspicious signs, the practitioner should immediately perform *homa* using the mantra of the Lord of the Red Body, or the *Jili-gira*, or the impure wrathful mantra; thus, the inauspicious signs shall be extinguished.
"Furthermore, a practitioner should not shave the hair of the three places; nor should they burn it, apply medicinal ointments to cause it to fall out, or pull it out by hand.
It is like a person holding a sharp blade: if they do not understand how to handle it well, they will surely harm themselves."

Upholding the immeasurable vidyās and various mantras taught by the World-Honored One, some among them belong to the Vajra Family, some belong to the Lotus Family, some belong to the Pañcika Family, some belong to the Maṇi Family, and some are likewise not subsumed within any family.
The various ritual rules and abbreviated instructions for mantras as explained above should all be practiced within these five families.
Furthermore, one should also practice those mantras spoken by the various devas that rely upon the World-Honored One.
If a practitioner rides upon this Dharma in such a manner, that rider shall achieve the fulfillment of their aspirations.

Furthermore, O World-Honored One, within the three realms of existence (triloka) there is the supreme and wondrous jewel; from this flows the ultimate Jewel of the Dharma, and from this are born the jewels of the eight great beings of the non-retrogressive assembly. These Three Jewels are what the world extols as jewels.

Therefore, if one who practices wishes to extinguish sins and generate merit so that the tutelary deity may swiftly appear before them, they should first take refuge in the Triple Gem at the beginning of their recitation.

Furthermore, if one recites a mantra belonging to the Vajra Family, after first taking refuge in the Triple Gem, they should next say: "Namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye," and then recite the mantra.
"Furthermore, the vidyās of the Lotus Family are likewise, as are those of the Pañcika Family, the Maṇi Family, and others.
One should first take refuge in the Triple Gem, then again take refuge in the Triple Gem, and next take refuge in the Lord of the Family; only after that may one recite and maintain the mantra."

If one does not place faith in the teachings of Śākyamuni, but instead practices the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, lacking sufficient faith, harboring internal decay while outwardly displaying diligence, and further maintaining stinginess—such a person should not uphold this Vaitulya teaching of mine.

If there should be a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā who disparages the profound and wondrous Mahāyāna, saying that what is taught therein is entirely the teaching of Māra; and if they further harbor ignorance, regarding the Vajradhara as a yakṣa, and fail to pay respectful homage to the great bodhisattvas—such a person who recites these sublime mantras shall, before long, naturally bring harm to their own life.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never harm sentient beings; however, within their retinues there are various classes of spirits who, seeing those deluded people mistakenly grasping the vajra-pestle, [intervene].

Furthermore, all the great divine kings dwelling on the earth, together with their retinues, descend here and each take their place in their respective directions. May they graciously accept the offerings I have prepared, and may they always protect me. By making such offerings to these spirits and the guardians of the directions, the practitioner will encounter no difficulties, and whatever aspirations they hold in mind will be entirely fulfilled.

12. The Twelfth Chapter: The Detailed Analysis of the Various Sections, Containing the Questions of the Youth Sumeru. Furthermore, Blessed One, for the benefit of sentient beings, you have taught three koṭis and five lakṣas of mantras and vidyās, which are called the Vidyādharapiṭaka.
Furthermore, the Noble Avalokiteśvara taught thirty-five million (350,000,000) mantras; within this family, the Lord of Mantras is named Hayagrīva, and the maṇḍala of this family is called Nivīya.

Furthermore, there are seven mantra-lords—namely, the twelve-armed mantra-lord, the six-armed, the crest-locked (Uṣṇīṣa), the one who fulfills all wishes, the four-faced, the Amoghapāśa, and the two-armed—who illuminate the world like the radiance of the sun.
These seven mantra-lords are all enshrined within the Hayagrīva maṇḍala.
Furthermore, there are eight vidyā-consorts, namely: Netrā, Śvetā, Upaśvetā, Avalokiteśvarī, Ekajaṭā, Suvarṇakapolā, Yaśovatī, and Bhṛkuṭī; these are all the vidyā-consorts within the Lotus Family.

Furthermore, various wonderful maṇḍalas and mudrās have been taught; for the sake of benefiting impoverished sentient beings and subduing the various classes of spirits, I have taught seventy million mantras and maṇḍalas.

"Furthermore, there are ten messengers, seven vidyārājñīs, sixty-four concubines, eight great heart-mantras, immeasurable wrathful deities such as Kuntali, and immeasurable mantra-lords such as the Supreme Vidyā; for these reasons, this family is called the Vast Bhadra-kalpa Family."

Furthermore, there is a great deity named Pañcika who speaks twenty thousand mantras; that deity has a consort named Mīḍhrola who speaks ten thousand mantras, and this is further called the Pañcika Section.
Furthermore, there is a great deity named Maṇibhadra who recites one hundred thousand mantras; the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa recites thirty thousand mantras; this is further known as the Maṇi Family.

Furthermore, there are devas and asuras who seek the principles of the Dharma and fully engage in its practice, reciting without interruption; such persons will swiftly attain accomplishment, be liberated from all sufferings, and further extinguish their transgressions, bestowing happiness upon both this life and future lives. Apart from the mantra, there is no other method whatsoever.
Just as when a celestial fire descends or frost and hail fall, they can damage all things and there is no way to escape them;
so too is the power of the mantra, which can destroy suffering and affliction, as well as all karmic obstacles.

Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel tree can fulfill the various aspirations of sentient beings, so too is the sublime Dharma of mantras; it can grant accomplishments, or bestow wealth and nobility, and it can provide physical strength, vitality, and long life in their entirety.

There are bodhisattvas who, observing sentient beings beset by various hardships and other terrors—such as the calamities of kings, wicked bandits, fire, hail, and other sufferings—immediately transform themselves into the form of a mantra-lord to rescue and protect those beings.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, though dwelling at home and enjoying various pleasures, does not neglect the rules of the Dharma taught within the mantras every day; and whether the number of recitations has not yet been fulfilled, or has been fulfilled at some time, or after a sign has appeared—such a person should immediately renounce the five desires, maintain pure and complete precepts, enter a clean room, and further recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. Thereafter, when seeking accomplishment (*siddhi*), they will before long attain the *mantra-siddhi* according to their heart's desire.

Furthermore, if the practitioner wishes to bathe, they should mix clean earth with water and smear it all over their body; thereafter, they enter the pure, flowing water and wash as they please, facing either east or north.

Having washed one's hands and feet, one should sit in the squatting posture (urdhvajānu), placing both hands between the knees. Having sprinkled water over the entire body, one must ensure the water makes no sound; then, using the right hand in the manner of scooping water, one should hold it in the palm so that no bubbles form, recite the mantra over the water three times, and swallow the water three times without making any noise.
Wipe the mouth twice with the thumb and sprinkle water over the body;

having thus performed the protection of the self, if one suddenly perceives a sensation of gaps between the teeth, impurities on the tongue, or coughing, spitting, or nasal mucus, or if one feels a pressure upon the chest, one must once again recite the mantra over water and drink it as described above.

Having finished rinsing the mouth and bathing, one should immediately proceed to a clean room; in the interim, one must not speak with or come into physical contact with any other outsiders—whether men or women, ordained persons, pure Brahmins, boys or girls, or eunuchs.
If there is physical contact [with another], one must again bathe as before and wipe the mouth with water; only then should one perform the recitation.

If one delights in bathing and subsequently delights in recitation, yet possesses compassion for all sentient beings and has no desire for the gains and offerings of others, and if, while eating by means of alms-gathering, the mantras are not according to the Dharma and one consequently gives rise to anger and harms their lives—[then one must likewise purify].

If there are those who uphold and recite the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras, and further are able to believe and accept them, as well as delighting in explaining them extensively for others, possessing courageous diligence and a firm, supreme resolve for bodhicitta—such persons, by reciting mantras, shall before long attain the accomplishment of their desired aims.
"What you have requested, I have already correctly explained for you as the complete teaching on the mantras of all the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, I shall speak incidentally of the teachings of the non-Buddhists; you should listen."

Maheśvara-deva has spoken ten koṭis of mantras; furthermore, all the various devas, nāgas, and their consorts have each spoken tens of millions of mantras, hand gestures (mudrās), and maṇḍalas. One should receive and maintain these according to the ritual rules; if one violates this teaching, not only will it fail to be accomplished, but it shall also bring about self-destruction.

13. The Thirteenth Section on the Analysis of the Eight Dharmas: The Inquiry of the Youth Sumāhu. "Furthermore, there are eight types of methods for achieving accomplishments in the world. They are: the method for accomplishing mantra-vidyās; the method for attaining longevity; the method for revealing hidden treasures; the method for entering the palaces of the asuras; the method for synthesizing gold; the method for turning earth into gold; the method for producing 'golden water'; and the method for producing priceless jewels. These are called the eight dharmas."
Within this, there are three superior methods:
the method for accomplishing mantra, the method for entering the palace of the asuras, and the method for attaining longevity; these three are the superior ones.
The method for accomplishing priceless jewels, the method for turning earth into gold, and the method for revealing hidden treasures—these three are the middling ones.
The method for compounding mercury with gold and the method for making "golden water"—these two are considered inferior.
If there are sentient beings who possess both ethical discipline and wisdom, and who likewise delight in the Dharma, such persons shall achieve the supreme accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings whose nature is characterized by much greed and desire, such persons achieve middling accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings who are much deluded, they achieve inferior accomplishment; one should not seek inferior accomplishment.
If one is left in poverty and lacks mastery over one's actions, one should seek the middling grade [of practice], yet still not seek the inferior.

If one wishes to obtain the various accomplishments described above, one must cultivate merit; for those who possess merit, whether they seek the happiness of humans and devas, or seek respect, mindfulness, longevity, long life, sovereign power, physical excellence, intelligence, and the capacity for retention, all such matters shall be successfully accomplished.
If one is free from attachment and delights in practicing virtuous conduct, keeping the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha constantly in mind, the same applies to the mantra-yakṣiṇīs.
Although they may dwell together, they ultimately harbor no good intentions; seeking out faults, they will surely cause harm.
Because of their ignorance, if they establish such a practice, not only do they commit the transgression of this perverse conduct, but they will also inevitably suffer harm themselves.

The mantras spoken by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, as well as those spoken before the Buddha by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and other such classes—all these the Tathāgata has fully authorized for the benefit of all sentient beings, and furthermore, he bestows his protective empowerment upon them.
These mantras all consist of three grades.

Those of the superior grade refer to ascending into the sky, entering the palaces of the asuras, transforming one's form at will, acting as a yakṣī or a lord of the heavens, remaining youthful throughout a long life, and through the power of transformation, manifesting oneself as Guhyapāda and others.
Those who achieve the middling grade obtain wealth and even attain nobility.
Those of the lower grade cause mutual increase among people, as well as being able to attract them; they can cause them to depart from their country, and even cause them to wither away.

Regarding the lowest of the low [methods]: for the purpose of curing afflictions by ghosts, demons, and the like—such as dragon-spirits, *nāga-mātṛkā*-spirits, or child-demons that cause people to fall into a stupor and sleep—one should recite the hand-gestures (*mudrā*), the pulling of the fists, the pushing, binding, and embracing, as well as the whispered instructions and the *āhvayeśana* [mantra]. One should then strike them to drive them away, even if they have caused harm; furthermore, one may have a multitude of people recite the mantra together, or have the people stamp their feet upon the ground.

Furthermore, they treat the poison of rats, restrain the members of their households, summon various nāgas, bind many people, cause crops not to grow, provide treatment for those afflicted by poison, are able to transfer poison, and bestow poison upon others.
Poison that has entered the human eye can likewise be treated.

For one who has been poisoned, a prohibition is established so that the snake cannot be led away; it is dispatched to harm another person, and it also manifests as a messenger. Such as these are external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*).

Furthermore, there are eighty species of venomous snakes; among them, twenty travel with their heads raised, and six of those die on the spot when they remain stationary. Among these, twelve species, though they bite, possess no venom.

Among the thirteen grounds within the numerical categories, there are residual snake-like beings outside [the ranks] who, though they may bite a person and occasionally inflict poison, [are ineffective against] such a person.

Because the dharma of the sublime mantra has clearly entered their bodies for the sake of seeking accomplishment, at the time of recitation, if there are donors who offer clothing, gold, silver, precious gems, saddles and mounts, ornaments, unguents, incense, food and drink, bedding, or any such items—even down to a single hair’s breadth—one should not accept them.

"Furthermore, after finishing the business of defecation and urination, one should use five portions of earth: three portions for washing after, one portion for washing before, and one portion for touching the hand while washing."

One should immediately leave the impure place and proceed to a clean spot to divide the earth into ten portions. First, use three portions to wash the left hand; then, use seven portions to wash both hands. Among these, first wash the inside of the left hand with three portions, one portion on the back of the hand, and subsequently wash both the inside and outside of both hands thoroughly with the remaining three portions until they are clean. Thereafter, use one’s discretion to apply earth and water to wash them until they are completely purified.

If one uses three clods of earth at the small place for excretion—two for the convenience of evacuation and one for washing upon contact—then at the cleansing place, one should again use three clods of earth to wash thoroughly once more.
For example, when the winds of spring rub against trees, fire naturally emerges; without effort, it burns all the grass.
In the same way, the fire of recitation, fanned by the wind of pure precepts and rubbed by the friction of diligence, completely consumes the grass of transgressions.
Furthermore, just as frost and dew vanish immediately when the sun shines, so too do the snows of sin dissolve through the radiant light of the recitation of precepts. It is also like this:

for example, if a room has been dark for a long time, the darkness is extinguished as soon as a lamp is brought inside; likewise, the lamp of recitation illuminates the body’s darkness of sin in exactly the same way.

If a practitioner recites mantras—even up to performing homa—and the mantra they maintain still does not succeed, they should use fragrant mud or clean sand near a river to respectfully construct one hundred thousand stūpa images. Thereby, the karmic obstructions created since beginningless time will be immediately extinguished, and in this very life, they shall attain accomplishment as a manifest retribution.

The method of mantra has ethical discipline as its root; next, there must be diligence and patience. One should harbor deep reverence toward all Buddhas, never allow the bodhicitta to regress, and remain free from indolence in one's recitation.

For example, just as a king who possesses seven qualities is able to govern his subjects and ensure his own peace and happiness, so too does a person who recites this [mantra] possess these seven qualities, whereby all sins are extinguished and they attain accomplishment.

First, one should perform the recitation of the mantra according to the Dharma; next, one should perform homa. Because of the homa, the tutelary deity becomes pleased and immediately bestows the accomplishment of one's aspirations.

"Furthermore, if one wishes to accomplish the dharmas for gathering and gladdening people—even those coming from as far as a hundred *yojanas* who are all wives of yakṣas—if, for the sake of desire, they become yakṣī women, even if they attain *siddhi*, they shall return to being wives of yakṣas."

For example, it is like a woman who sells her beauty and engages in lust with others for the sake of looking at their wealth; driven by hunger, she seizes and strikes sentient beings, causing their minds to become disordered. She may sing or dance, be joyful or sorrowful, harbor distress, or speak incoherently at times—manifesting various such strange signs that cause people to marvel and laugh. One should immediately treat this condition with the Vajra-Hook mantra, or the mantras of the Amṛta-vase or the Wrathful Vajra, so that they may be healed and cured.

Furthermore, there are the mantras of the Fire God, the Wind God, Maheśvara, the Sun and Moon deities, Mahābrahmā, the Dragon Kings, Nārāyaṇa, Vaiśravaṇa, the various Yakṣa kings, the Garuḍa kings, and the Trāyastriṃśa kings; yet these spirits and demons do not fear such other external deities as they do when they hear the name of the Vajrāṅkuśa, for they naturally disperse and retreat.
The wise one, knowing the nature and conduct of those malevolent spirits as well as the methods for their treatment, subsequently subdues them without fear.
The mantras spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are empowered by the Tathāgata; thus, the various mantras of other external deities cannot destroy the mantras of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, if one wishes to extinguish transgressions, one should, in a secluded and quiet place, construct a *caitya* using fragrant mud or sand near a river; within it, one should install the verse on the Dharmakāya of Dependent Origination.

At that time, the Brahma King, the various devas, yakṣas, vidyādhara maharṣis, garuḍas, gandharvas, bhūtas, and other such beings, having seen and heard this Dharma, paid homage with prostrations; they simultaneously joined their palms and spoke these words:

"How rare, O Venerable One, is your compassion for sentient beings! How rare is such a subtle and supreme practice! We see you sometimes holding a blazing, great *vajra*; sometimes holding a firm iron pestle; sometimes holding a fierce and sharp great wheel; sometimes we see you holding the *Amoghapāśa* lasso; sometimes we see you holding a three-pronged trident; sometimes we see you holding a great scimitar; sometimes we see you holding a bow; sometimes we see you holding a staff; or we see you equipped with various weapons, extraordinary, terrifying, and rare; or we see you with marks and signs so upright and majestic as to be delightful to all who behold you. Or we see the Venerable One acting as a Yakṣa general. To such a Bodhisattva, revered by devas, asuras, and others, we take refuge."
If there are people who take refuge in the Venerable One, they will before long attain the status of a great vidyādhara-sage and even wealth and nobility.
If there are those who practice such a True Dharma, they will swiftly be freed from the great suffering of poverty.
The majestic radiance... is sometimes without poison.
Furthermore, there are various species such as frogs, lizards, chameleons, *zhā*, *luán*, and spiders, as well as those that act as venomous insects.
Although such classifications are numerous, the types of poison they inflict are sixfold: first, the mere contact of their excrement with the body brings forth poison;

second, the contact of their urine with the body brings forth poison; third, the contact of their touch with the body brings forth poison; fourth, the contact of their discharge, excrement, or saliva with the body brings forth poison; fifth, the mere gaze of their eyes brings forth poison; and sixth, the contact of their teeth brings forth poison. These various poisons are further divided into superior, middling, and inferior grades, resulting in many varieties; for this reason, other deities and gods have taught these methods, such as the mantras for curing poison.

Thus, these various insects release fierce venom either because they are intoxicated by poison, or out of anger, or out of fear, or due to hunger, or because they harbor resentment, or because the time of their death has arrived.
The poisons from their bites are further of four kinds:
first, injury; second, blood-staining; third, extreme damage; and fourth, death.
Where there is a single tooth mark at the site of the bite and the poison is slight, it is called "injury."
Where the bite leaves two tooth marks causing blood to flow, it is called "blood-smeared" (*rudhirārdra*).
Where the bite leaves three tooth marks causing injury to the interior, it is called "extremely damaged" (*atipātita*).

Wherever it bites, four tooth-marks appear and immediately envelop the body; this is called the end of life. This single poison cannot be cured or remedied even by means of mantras or sublime medicines.
It is like a fierce fire burning the body, or being cut with a blade; one who has been poisoned is likewise.
If one were to treat it with medicine, it would not equal the power of a mantra. Just as when a great fire breaks out and is extinguished by sprinkling rain, so too does a mantra subdue poison.

The wise one possesses a profound understanding of the various types of poisons and likewise recites the mantra of great majesty; thus, they sport with all manner of poisons without the slightest fear, just as a lion enters a herd of cattle.

Furthermore, there are various types of possessing spirits—such as those of devas, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, vidyādharas, gandharvas, pretas, piśācas, and others—who roam the world for the sake of seeking sacrifices, or out of a desire to mock, or for the purpose of killing. They constantly devour flesh and blood, watching for and seeking out faults.
Whether out of anger they strike or seize sentient beings, or due to afflictions, or because of famine in the world appearing like the sun,
we shall protect such practitioners so that their minds do not become distracted, and they shall constantly attain the accomplishment of their wishes.
After the Brahma Kings and the other devas had spoken these words, they were filled with great joy; they prostrated themselves at his feet, each mounting their great seats, and withdrew to depart.
